result.reason: Both items are the opening lines of the Mishnah prohibiting mixing produce (even new with new, and certainly new with old), which is precisely what the 'Mishnah: No Mixing' prose describes.

The passage covers both the wine-mixing exception (strong with weak) and the lees rule in a single Mishnaic statement, and candidate 0 ('Wine Exception') introduces the mixing permission while candidate 1 covers only the lees portion — but since the entire quoted text is one unified Mishnaic passage, it fits best under its current placement which introduces the exception that encompasses the full statement.

The passage covers the complete Mishnah text about diluted wine disclosure, the merchant restriction, and the local custom exception — matching the current placement under 'Diluted Wine Disclosure' which quotes this exact Mishnah opening, while the subsequent headings cover only individual sub-topics of the same Mishnah.

The passage describes the merchant/wholesaler taking grain from five threshing floors and wine from five winepresses into one storage facility, which is precisely what the 'Middleman Mixing' section's prose discusses.

Both items are explicitly discussed in the 'Grain Price Reversal' prose, which covers the baraita about new/old grain pricing and then the wine exception with Rabbi Elazar's derivation about 'be-emet amru' — exactly matching the content of both items.

The passage is Rav Naḥman's statement about the pressing season (bein ha-gitot) being the context for permitted wine-mixing, which directly matches the 'Wine Pressing Times' section's prose about this very qualification.

The passage directly discusses the modern practice of mixing wine outside pressing season and the opinions of Rav Pappa and Rabbi Aḥa, which is exactly what the 'Modern Wine Practice' prose section describes.

Both items directly address the Gemara's analysis of the lees-mixing prohibition and Rav Yehuda's clarification — the exact content described in candidate 0's prose about *ein me'arvin shmarim shel emesh be-shel yom* and what *noten lo et shmarav* means.

The passage contains the full narrative unit — Rava receiving wine, Abaye's objection, and Rava's defense — which all belongs under 'Rava's Situation' (index 1), the heading whose prose describes this entire episode, rather than being split across multiple headings.

The passage discusses local customs for diluting wine with standard ratios (half, third, quarter) and Rav's note about the pressing season, which matches the 'Dilution Standards' prose that explicitly references these same ratios and local practice expectations.

The passage is the Mishna itself covering both the gifts-to-children ruling and the price-undercutting ruling, and it currently sits under 'Gifts to Children' whose prose directly introduces and discusses this exact Mishnaic text.

The passage covers exactly what heading 3 'Bean Sifting' discusses — Abba Shaul's prohibition on sifting ground beans, the Rabbis' permission, their concession about the bin opening deception, and the beautification ban — all of which are introduced in that section's prose.
The passage directly presents the Gemara's reasoning for the Rabbis' permission of treats for children (nuts vs. jujubes), which is precisely what the 'Treats Logic' section's prose describes.

All three items — the Rabbis' praise for lowering market price and the identification of 'the Rabbis' in the Abba Shaul dispute as Rabbi Acha — are explicitly discussed in the 'Price Praise' prose, making it the clear and correct placement.

The passage contains both the mishna about adorning persons/animals/vessels AND the baraita listing the three forbidden practices (mesharvitin, nofchin, shorin), plus the Gemara's brief inquiry into mesharvitin's meaning — all of which together map directly onto 'Beautification Examples' prose, which describes exactly these three forbidden practices and their context, whereas 'Mesharvitin Meaning' prose only discusses the definitional inquiry, not the full passage.

The passage contains the full sequence of Sages' permissions AND the resolution of the contradiction with the Mishnah (chadtei vs. atikei), which is precisely what heading 3 'Old vs New' discusses — the governing distinction that resolves the apparent conflict.
The passage describes the elderly slave dyeing his hair to appear young and approaching Rava to be purchased, which is precisely what the 'Old Slave Case' prose discusses.

The passage describes exactly the events discussed in candidate 0's prose: the slave going to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, the water-fetching incident, the revealed white hair, and Rav Pappa applying the verse about the righteous being delivered from trouble.

The Hadran formula marks the conclusion of chapter Ha-zahav, which is explicitly what the prose under 'End Ona'ah' describes — concluding Ha-zahav and the ona'ah discussion before transitioning to the next perek.

The passage is the mishna that introduces and poses the question 'Which is neshekh and which is tarbit?' — matching the 'Neshech & Tarbit' section's prose about the two terms and their definitions, before the mishna answers with specific examples covered under 'Neshech Example'.
The passage directly presents the Mishnah's definition of neshech with the sela/five-dinar and two se'ah/three se'ah examples, which is precisely what the 'Neshech Example' prose discusses.

Both items together describe the tarbit case where grain prices rise and the seller converts the grain obligation into a wine obligation he doesn't possess — exactly what the 'Price Rise Problem' prose discusses in detail, including the thirty-dinar valuation, the wine conversion, and the lack of wine in the seller's possession.

The passage directly presents the Gemara's inference that neshekh and tarbit are one matter on the Torah level (michlal de-Oraisa chada milsa hi), and then raises the challenge from the verses — both of which are precisely what the 'Single Category' prose describes and analyzes.

All five items form the continuous Gemara discussion of whether neshekh and tarbit can exist independently — the currency depreciation and appreciation hypotheticals with their resolutions — which is precisely what the 'Currency Example' heading's prose describes.

The passage is Rava's conclusion that neshech and tarbis always co-occur and the Torah distinguished them only to create two prohibitions, which is exactly what candidate 0's prose is discussing and directly quotes.

The passage covers exactly the content described in heading 0's prose — the Leviticus verse establishing neshech by money and ribit by food, and the question of where neshech by food is derived — which is precisely where it currently sits.

The passage describes the hermeneutical move (im eino inyan) redirecting the redundant 'neshekh of money' to teach that ribbit/marbis applies to money as well, which is precisely what the 'Derived Prohibitions' prose section discusses.
